content: The hypothesis that garlic might play a role in preventing pre-eclampsia and its complications is based on its potential to lower blood pressure, inhibit platelet aggregation, and reduce oxidative stress. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of garlic on the prevention of pre-eclampsia and its associated complications. A search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of January 2010. Randomized trials assessing the effects of garlic on pre-eclampsia prevention were included. Two independent reviewers selected the trials and extracted the data, which were analyzed using Review Manager software. The data were cross-verified for accuracy. One trial involving 100 women of uncertain methodological quality compared garlic supplementation with a placebo. Another study was excluded due to a high dropout rate, with 29% of participants lost to follow-up. The results showed no significant difference between the garlic and placebo groups in the risk of developing gestational hypertension (relative risk [RR] 0.50, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.25 to 1.00) or pre-eclampsia (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.93). Women who received garlic were more likely to report experiencing odour compared to those in the placebo group (RR 8.50, 95% CI 2.07 to 34.88). However, no significant differences were observed in other reported side effects. The only other outcomes reported in the study were the rate of caesarean section (RR 1.35, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.95) and perinatal mortality. Notably, there were no perinatal deaths reported in the trial. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend increased garlic intake for the prevention of pre-eclampsia and its complications. While garlic was associated with odour as a side effect, no serious adverse effects were reported. Larger, high-quality randomized trials are necessary to further evaluate the effects of garlic before any clinical recommendations can be made.
